formal.statement: theorem Int.induction_on : ((x0 : ((x0 : Int) -> Prop)) -> ((x1 : x0 Int.zero) -> ((x2 : ((x2 : Int) -> ((x3 : x0 x2) -> x0 (Int.add x2 Int.one)))) -> ((x3 : ((x3 : Int) -> ((x4 : x0 x3) -> x0 (Int.sub x3 Int.one)))) -> ((x4 : Int) -> x0 x4)))))

notes:
The interesting measurement is that this was CHEAP, against a lane's prior sizing of 'genuinely comparable-or-more effort than the theorem it blocks'. The integers' operations are nested Int.rec over the naturals, so at a CONSTRUCTOR argument every bridging step below computes and no equation lemma is needed anywhere:
  add (ofNat k) one   reduces to  ofNat (succ k)      -- Nat.add recurses on its right argument and that argument is the literal 1
  sub zero one        reduces to  negSucc 0           -- Int.sub is a plain Definition; subNatNat scrutinises the closed Nat.sub 1 0
  sub (negSucc k) one reduces to  negSucc (succ k)    -- again the literal is on the right
So the proof is two Nat.rec inductions whose terms have DEFINITIONALLY the types the kernel expects, and add_declaration's own defeq check closes each one. It was accepted on the first attempt. This is also why the downward step is stated with Int.sub rather than in the P (n+1) -> P n form: sub costs nothing here and is what a caller wants to write.

First consumer: Int.fib_add (F:ml430-int-fib-add-181b6a2c), whose two-step recurrence needs the paired motive P k and P (k+1) on top of this.

prior_art.attribution: Mathlib's Int.induction_on indexes both steps by a NATURAL (forall i : N, p i -> p (i+1) and forall i : N, p (-i) -> p (-i-1)), which is strictly stronger as a theorem and less convenient at a use site. The form here quantifies both steps over the INTEGERS. Neither Mathlib's statement nor its proof was consulted; the construction is this kernel's own.

statement: Int.rec splits an integer into ofNat n and negSucc m and hands back a NATURAL in each branch: it is a case split, not an induction principle for the integers. Int.induction_on is the induction principle -- prove a motive at 0, step upward by add n one and downward by sub n one, conclude it at every integer. Nothing in the integer development inducted over the integers before it; statements whose index arithmetic crosses zero (Int.fib_add) had no route, and the magnitude-decided workaround (push to natAbs, as Int.fib_of_odd does) does not apply to them.
title: Int.induction_on -- two-sided induction over the constructed integers
